01.r: Joins the widow's arrival to the scene at the treasury.

02.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having come', joined to the main verb; English joins the two with 'and'.

03.r: Singles out one woman from the crowd of givers.
03.n: The numeral 'one'. The KJV and Geneva take it as 'a certain', the ASV and YLT as plain 'a'; this study keeps the numeral, as the BSB does.

04.r: A woman whose husband has died.
04.n: Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses this word chiefly for Hebrew אַלְמָנָה, widow.

05.n: Abbott-Smith derives the word from πτώσσω, 'to crouch, cower', and gives 'a beggar' as its sense when used as a noun. The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew עָנִי, among other words for the poor.

06.r: She puts her coins into the treasury.
06.n: Abbott-Smith gives the range 'to throw, cast, put, place'. This study renders it 'cast' throughout the treasury scenes, so the reader can follow the one verb through Mark and Luke.

07.r: Two of the smallest coins in use.
07.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from λέπω, 'to peel': the adjective means fine, thin, small, and in late Greek τὸ λεπτόν is a small coin, one-eighth of an as. This study keeps the coin's own name, lepton (plural lepta); 'mite' is the KJV's English equivalent.

08.r: Two coins, both of the smallest kind.

09.r: Refers to the two lepta taken together.
09.n: Neuter singular: the two coins are reckoned as one sum.

10.n: Singular in the Greek, agreeing with 'which': the two together 'is' one quadrans.

11.r: A small Roman coin, used to state the value of the two lepta.
11.n: Abbott-Smith explains it as the Latin quadrans, 'the fourth part of an as', the AV's 'farthing'; his figures agree, since two lepta at one-eighth of an as make a quarter. Mark states the Greek coins' value in Roman money, likely for readers who reckoned in it; that is an inference. The BSB's 'a small fraction of a denarius' explains rather than translates.
t: a small fraction of a denarius
